st.—They are in favour of giving the tenants legal and compulsory com- pensation for unexhausted improve- ments, and at least a year's notice to quit.
2nd.—They will vote for the re- form of the laws affecting the owner- ship and transfer of land. I 3rd.—They will vote for the aboli- tion of the laws of distress and hypothec.

Teen eunteet in Mid-Cheehire is being pronecuted with much vigour by both political partice. Bo far the Liberals have reason to be nattsfied with their pro- jo,l4l in the campaign, and the Connervative candid.. betray in their speech., a realination of the fact that a change has come over the minds of the farming community Aillee the loot election. Coupled with the discovery that under the ballot the vote, of farmer. are an secret en it in pegmatite to make them, sgrinultur. tete, who have been befooled to the top of their bent by the vain promises of the Tories, are beginning to see that if an improvement of their condition is to be aecompliehed by legislation, that legislation must and will come from , the Liberal party. In the pest, tanners have been led to look solely to the Toriee for such legislation. They have beau allured by the generono promisen of the Beaconsfield party, and been deceived; and now the Torten would have them homiwinked Commn by similar promises. Su•th attention rte the present Government have bentowed on :natters affecting agriculturist, whilet active in creating jealousies and distrunt all over the gibe, has ended in failure. We have in theoe nolumns more than once shown the Agricultural Holdings Act of the prenent Government to be a farce : their Cattle Diseases Bill won a nibterable failure in no far no it met the desires of fanners or protected the inmrentn of meat eonnumerti ; and their pledgee to relieve farmer. of their burdens of taxation have proved hollow pretence, An Mr. Goetthen recently observed, "They found local mxation in a mata of confunion and chaos, and after 81S yearn of power, though backed by a large nmjerity, they left thin im- portant subject where they found it." The County Government Bill, in connection with which the Tories wombed to secure to farmers the same control over the expenditure of the rates they paid that, in posseseed by the inhabitants of boroughs, tone great an abortion as the other meaeuree by which protessed advantages were dangled before the eyee of the voters in tho agricul- tural districts. Remembering all theme broken pledgee, and that the Government has multiplied mimplioations all over the world, that the /3.conefield policy h. Intensified the depremion in trade, th it farmers are no longer boned hand and (mit to follow the political , dictates of landlord, and that in the coming Parlia- mono the Liberal perty will concede to the agriculture bite rightn and privileges Torten promised but withheld, the voter, of Mid-Cheshire and the other divietions of tlxit county will find it to their inter'sot tot support at the ballot box the return of the Liberal candidates. Let there be no misunderstanding that the voter in by the ballot thoroughly protected. His landlord may dictate, but the vote] may drop his voting paper into the ballot boa with tae satisfaction that no one will discover how he has voted if he will only keep his own couneel.

In season and out of meson Mr. Latham has been • anlonli advocate for the extension of just laws to the farming ..lass, and no man will enter the Honey of Commons better acquainted with the inequalitts id the land-lawe than he is. South-West Lancashire still prefer, tooling to Toryism. notwithstanding that all along toe line, from north to e mth from east to west, constituency after constituency hat thrown off the yoke of Tory repratentation and given wel- come by large majoritiee to a reign of Liberalism. Undo the changed aspect of political parties, the Conservatives have to rejoice over small mercies: and seeing that constitu- ency after constituency has been swept out of their hands by the broad and strong wave of Liberalism positing over ! the country, it is not to be wondered at that they should have been frantic with delight on Wednesday when it was announced that they had been successful in retaining their hold upon the South-wesMrn division of the county of Lancaster. It was to them a crumb of comfort, and they rejoiced over it immeasurably, their delight find- ing expression in H.. ringing of bells, the !morning ot cannon, and the blow., of wind instruments. That the victory hat been amble, eil by thein was in sonde degree matter of aurprise to the Conservatives themselvw. The most sanguine of their body had looked forward to Colonel Blackburne being remitted to Hale Hall. and to Mr. Cross and Mr. Rathbone being reelected to represent the division in Sc. Stephen's. If Liberals felt persuaded that the victory would be theirs, t hey felt convinced that it could only he secured by a small Imajority. They fought gallantly, and were beaten. It is I gratifying to tind that t e two gentlemen who championed 1 the Liberal ranee took their defeat good burnouredly, and that whilst conceding to their opponents the right of I befing jubilant,—not over securing an additional mat, but over simply maintaining their hold upon what they hail previously possessed the Liberal cmdidates and their supporters found abundant coneolation in the fact that on the same day the Tory victory in Pooch- Wolf Lincasbire was announced another division of the county palatine—the South-Eastern--gave to the Secretary to the Admiralty, Mr. Alge-non Egerton, and Mr. Edward Harken', the late members, unmisMkable notice to give up possesaion of their seats to Messrs. Leake and Agnew, both Liberate. The victory won by the two latter gentlemen ion full and eatisfactory mower to all the boast- inge of the Conservatives in South-West L....hire, maintaining their hold upon that division. But the Libera, achievements did not cod here, for on the same day Mr. Jas. Howard, the farmers' candidate, rode into power in Bedford. shire, at the head of the poll and Mr. Welkin Williams drove out a Conservative in Carnarvmshire. Seats in Ave burghs, Berwickshire, East Derbyshire, South Norfolk, North Notts., Radnorshire, South Warwickshire, Peebleashire, I North Staffordahire, West CurnbetLand, Wicklow, Ac, were I wised by the Liberals from Tory holders. Throughout the whole of the diviaion of South-West Lance- Ishire the partisans of the respective candidates worked vigorously, early and late, and we regret to , notice that at one or two places, but more especially Widnes, the excitement consequent upon the election ended in brawls and damage to property. St. Helena, Warrington, Preacnt, ' indeed throughout the whole division the utmost vigilance , was displayed by Liberal workers; and it will be men from I : a report, we give elsewhere, that a large percentage of the voters in the various polling dietrient were brought to the poll. In the face of the magnificent victories which the Liberal, have gained in the boroaghs, and are now reaping in the counties, it is undoubtedly to be regretted that South- West Lancashire should have adhered to the old state of Ithings still it is essential. that there should be an opposi- ; tics in the House of Commons, and. for aught we know, Mr. Cress and Colonel Blackburne are as likely to do as little mischief on the Opposition benches as any other two men the constituency of South-West Lancaahire could have chomen to represent the "gunpowder and glory policy " in a House of Commons pledged to "Peace, Retrenchment, and Reform."

Monday an In- quest was held by Mr. Worsley, deputy coroner, at Die Iferby Arms, kept by Mr. Tin.ley, on this body of Hannah Wil- cock, aged 39, of Fryer-street.—Phi.lip Thompson Wilcock, who is about 13 years old, and is employed at the ropewalk, said lie was the son of deceased, and when she went to bed, on Saturday night, about eleven o'clock, she wee perfectly ' sober. Near one o'clock in the morning he heard some one knocking at the door, on which his mother got out of bed, I went to the top of the Maim, and mid" Who's there?" He heard a man's voice, in reply, saying "It's only no let Isle in." His (witness's) mother Answered " Well, I'm not going to let you in," undue mon sr she had said them words she fell down stair.. Ile and his sister then got the lamp and went to me what was amis.. They found their mother lying upon her side at the bottom of the Claire, and they saw some blood on the door. They mcceeded in taking de- ceaeed upstairs and putting her into bed, lie spoke to her, but she made no answer. and he then went for one el the neighbours. At about half-past eight he found hie mother was dying, and he fetched the neighbours into the boom ag.tin. Decomed died ehortly afterwards.—Mrs. Eliza Uri nes, wife of Ssenuelr Grimes, labourer, liranville-street, deposed that on Sundry morning the last witness came to her and asked if ehe would go to me his mother, who had fallen down emirs and wee badly hurt. She found her upon the bed, and she appeared as if asleep. Deceased made no reply to her questions. There was blood upon the Maim Ind on deceased's hair and drees. 1/n visiting her again, letween seven and eight o'clock, she found her breathing very hard. She went for demurs uncle. Deceased died • Mort time after she arrived at the house, where she re- mained afoul half-an-hour.—ln answer to the coroner, win. ems. said she did trot rend for a doctor, as she had no authority to do no, end if she had taken it upon hermit she might have been asked to pay the charge of the medical man —Florence Wilcock. an intelligent girl, the daughter of demised, corroborated the matement of her brother.—'Fhe coroner said the jury, who had vieited the house, would agree with him that the dep.., at the top of which the poor woman was standing when she tell, were sufficiently steep to make them dangerous for the most steady and collected person. Ile alert remarked that he thought it would hays been much better if Mrs. Grimm had rent fora doctor.—Tbe jury returned a verdict of Accidental death."—After Borne remarks by one of the jurymen, the Coroner said his atten- tion had been called to the fact that in the sleeping room of the family the occupants must have slept slain a ked, when the husband was at home. He muet say that this was a very direagremble State of things.—Mr. Broadhurst (grocer): I think that in cases like that our Inspector of Nuisances ought at once to make a report to the Commissioners.— Another juryman expreesed the opinion that wherever in the town there were such came of overcrowding it was the duty of the !week, .4 N. irtancee and the Medical Officer of Health to report them AI once. What was the use of haying those officers if they did not prevent such terrible over- crowding, which was Co likely to breed disease. A. to the man who owned the house—Mr. Let, furniture broker, and

The evidence of Mrs. Ann Atherton, the wile of Mr. Ralph Atherton, of the Camden Hotel, Surreyetreet, and Sarah Ainecough, the wife of deceased. showed that deceased had for a considerable time been suffering from dropsv and heart disease. He heat been under a doctor at Sowerhy Bridge, and also at.ndel by the assistant to Dr. Robinson, of Bantam. The doctors agreed as to the nature of the complaints from which he was suffering. On the previous Wednesday the wife of deceased went to Liverpool, at his request, to fetch a boy home. Deceased was then in a mer- rier state of mind than she had seen him for Nome tirne. She returned on Saturday, hut found that the door had been burst open by Mrs. Atherton and the neighbour., and Ain. cough found dead in bed The jory returned . verdict or j Natural causes."—Whilst the evidence in the ease me.; being taken, Inspector Dutton handfd to the coroner an information as to the body of a man, then unknown, and ahotatlb years of age, baying been found in what is known as the house basin at the Bottom Locks The body appeared to have been in the water for about a fortnight. It was in a very advanced state of decorepoeit ion, and wan then lying at the Bridgewa.r Arms Hotel. He thotiat It would be • greet advantage if it could be removed to some other place. Mr. Richard Howie', keeper of the New Inn, who wan acting on the jam, said there eras a large family of young children bring at the house, and it was highly important that a body which was in such an advanced stete of decomposition should be removed. He Imes personally what it was some- times to be put in a similar position to the keeper of the Bridgewater Arms. He thought that the Commissioners ought to undertake to do anything in relation to providing a place to which bodies found ender euch circumetances I !coold be taken. The Coroner remarked that he quite agreed with the observations of the witnew ; but he felt convinced that, however many complaints might be made they would I I have no effect until each neglect bad caused an epidemic of typhus fever in the town. The foreman of the jury con- aiderei it highly important that the Commissioners should consider the repeated applications which Mil been made to them to provide a d.d-house. The inepector was requested to see Mr. Wright, relieving officer, 5 to having the body washed, so that if there were eny marks of violence upon it I the police might be made aware of the feet. Shortly after- ! ward, be returned, and stated he had found that he could hare the t.ly put in a shed close to the public-house. He had seen the relieving officer, who had told him that he could do nothing but see to the burial of the baiy. Mr. Wright said he ehoold not have it washed " or de enything of the sort," as he had no power to order anything but the burial. He (the inspector), however. knew that the relieving officer had the requisite power, for where he had been stationed before coming to Runcorn —at Northwich and other places—the relieving officers had seen to this work being done. A juryman I think it has been done on previous occasions The Coroner The resole will be that I ehall order a post-mortem examination, end the body will hare to be washed for that. The foreman of the any, at the close of the proceedings, said he had enquired of the gentlemen empanelled, and he found that there was a wrong desire amongst them that a mortuary should be provided by the Commissioners. Thie was not the first time that thi, ques- tion had been brought prominently before a noncom jury. The jury wished that the coroner would make a representa- tion to the Commissioners upon the subject. The coroner, said he wax much obliged to the foreman for callMgattenth n both. matter, as he looked upon the provision of • menu., I as an absolute neceseity.—This terminated the proceedings both, ans.

Plyef,A, on Saturday night, egress from the building was I next to impossible owing to the dense toss, of roughs as- sembled to prevent them. 'I he too policemen merited totally powerlese to prevent injury 10th, people, but great praise is due to them, under Superintendent Brindle and Sergeants 'Bull and Crawford, for the fm bearance and patience dim • played by them during the tumult. A torchlight procession had been arranged, headed by the Presoot Loud Bran Band, but it was found to be totally impracticable. Some 00 or 1 70 lighted torches fortunabdy shed a good light around, and I that prevented more serious injury. Nome little time was I lott in conseyence of many of the torches becoming extin- guished before the conclusion of the meeting At length the eign.il to march wari given, but before half a dozen steno had been taken in the direction of Church.etreet, the mob darted in upon the torch bearers, and a scene of inextricable coot union ensued. The to to, armed with wooden inalleta, !Ac., engaged in indiscriminare fighting whoever they came ; in contact. and niany gentlemen suffered injuries in cone. quence, who had been present at the meeting. The police oriel every exertion on their part to reetore order, but with. out avail. Mrs. Evan, the chairman's wife, was escorted to I her reeidence by them, and fortunately suffeved no injury. AUSTRALIA. BIMBANE, Apan. 6.—The re,.e returns of this colony ,1 for the year ending March 31 show an increase of £30.000 i as compared with the same period of last year, combined with a saving of expenditure to the like amount. The in- awned receipts are derivable mainly from the railways and ' the land revenue. The imports and exports show little change in comparison with the first three months of 1879.1 The produce of sugar in the colony during lost year: amounted to 19000 tons, and with regard to wool the oflicial reports declare last clip Co have been superior in every respect to that of the preceding season. Parmers' prospects generally for this year are regarded as excellent, and the season very favourable, throughout the colony. FRANCE.
